claims.text: A Pulumi blog post titled 'SST Runs on the Pulumi Engine: What It Means to Build on Pulumi' exists at /blog/sst-built-on-pulumi/ and covers the engine mechanics behind SST's migration to Pulumi.
AWS CDK tied infrastructure to AWS.
Multi-cloud was nearly impossible with AWS CDK.
In its early days, SST was built on top of AWS's Cloud Development Kit (CDK), which allowed developers to define infrastructure using TypeScript or Python.

AWS CDK and CloudFormation act as a code generator, producing an intermediary format (YAML or JSON) that is then executed to deploy resources, so the code the developer writes is not the code running during deployment.
AWS CDK supports only AWS, while Pulumi supports AWS, Azure, GCP, and on-premises.
Pulumi offers real-time debugging, whereas debugging AWS CDK is hard due to CloudFormation.
AWS CDK supports only TypeScript and Python, while Pulumi supports any programming language.
Pulumi deployments are faster than AWS CDK deployments because CDK is slowed by CloudFormation.
AWS CDK uses a CloudFormation state file, whereas Pulumi uses Pulumi-managed state.
AWS CDK supports only AWS Secrets Manager for secrets management, while Pulumi has cross-cloud secret support.
Pulumi offers custom providers and workflows for extensibility, while AWS CDK extensibility is limited to the AWS ecosystem.
Pulumi treats infrastructure code as a first-class program executed directly during deployment instead of generating an intermediary format.

A Founding Engineer at SST said: 'With Pulumi, the deployment process feels like a natural extension of writing code - it's intuitive and powerful and capable of advanced things that traditional IaC tools can't handle.'
Pulumi Insights (product/pulumi-insights page) provides improved visibility and debugging capabilities for deployments.
Pulumi has built-in extensibility features including custom providers and dynamic components.
With CDK/CloudFormation, SST had to resort to hacky workarounds or custom Lambda functions to customize deployment.
Pulumi lets you define infrastructure in TypeScript, Python, Go, or C# and deploy across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and on-premises environments from one workflow.
Pulumi Cloud Deployments (docs/pulumi-cloud/deployments) exists and supports advanced deployment workflows.
Pulumi Crosswalk for AWS simplifies 'day one' tasks, and an AWS guide exists at /docs/iac/guides/clouds/aws/.
An on-demand workshop titled 'Getting Started with Infrastructure as Code on AWS' exists at pulumi.com/resources/getting-started-with-iac-pulumi-aws/.
SST is a framework that makes building modern full-stack applications on your infrastructure easy.
Ion is the code name for a new SST engine that deploys SST components using Pulumi instead of CDK and CloudFormation.
Once Ion is stable, it will be released as SST v3.
SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for its providers and deployment engine, and bridges Terraform providers through Pulumi.
SST makes money primarily through its managed service, SST Console.
The SST Console is optional and includes a free tier.
SST v3 replaced AWS CDK and CloudFormation with an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make the underlying cloud API calls.
Running `sst deploy` does not require a Pulumi account or Pulumi Cloud dependency.
The Pulumi engine ships inside the SST CLI, so running `sst deploy` requires no separate Pulumi install.
SST keeps its deployment state in an S3 bucket in the user's own AWS account rather than in Pulumi Cloud.
SST v3 is the Ion-based rewrite of the SST framework.
The SST team has said, repeatedly since the rewrite shipped, that SST's architecture is built on the Pulumi engine.
SST is an open source TypeScript framework from the team formerly known as Serverless Stack.
SST can build and deploy full-stack applications to AWS and more than 150 other providers.

In SST, app infrastructure and code are defined together in a single `sst.config.ts` file using SST's own components (functions, queues, buckets, static sites), and `sst deploy` handles provisioning end to end.
Through 2023, SST's provisioning layer was built directly on AWS CDK and CloudFormation.
In late 2023 the SST team began a rewrite, code-named Ion, that replaced SST's entire deployment layer.
Ion shipped as SST v3 in mid-2024.
Ion (SST v3 architecture) has been the only supported SST architecture since it shipped.

SST's blog post 'Moving away from CDK' says: "Ion is a code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications. The constructs (or components) are defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi; as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation (CFN)."

SST's blog post 'Moving away from CDK' says: "When you run `sst deploy`, those resources make a call to an embedded Pulumi engine that makes a call to their bridged Terraform provider, and this makes the AWS SDK calls to create your resources."
The SST docs ('What is SST') say: "SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine. And Terraform's providers are bridged through Pulumi."
Independent developers who compared SST, Terraform, and Pulumi directly describe SST as built on the Pulumi engine.

Gautier Blandin's article 'Terraform, Pulumi, SST: a tradeoff analysis' says: "SST uses the Pulumi engine under the hood to manage and provision resources, and lets users write Pulumi code in addition to using SST's constructs, enabling resources with no associated SST constructs to still be defined and deployed."

Kiryl Anoshka's dev.to article 'SST ditches AWS CDK. Time to move on to Ion' says: "You may notice right away the imports from Pulumi. It means the whole deployment process will be built on Pulumi now."

The published `package.json` for SST's platform package depends on `@pulumi/pulumi`, plus first-party Pulumi providers for AWS, Cloudflare, Docker builds, and more, alongside a Pulumiverse Vercel provider.

SST's `platform/package.json` lists `@pulumi/pulumi`, `@pulumi/aws`, `@pulumi/cloudflare`, `@pulumi/command`, `@pulumi/docker-build`, `@pulumi/random`, `@pulumi/tls`, and `@pulumiverse/vercel` as direct dependencies.
The SST repository is now at `anomalyco/sst` (formerly `sst/sst`).
In SST's deploy chain, `sst deploy` reads `sst.config.ts`, resolves SST components, and those components compile into Pulumi resource declarations.
The Pulumi engine diffs desired vs. actual state, builds a dependency graph, and orders operations.
Terraform-bridged providers translate each Pulumi resource into cloud API calls, via Pulumi's Terraform bridge (github.com/pulumi/pulumi-terraform-bridge).
Pulumi's engine owns dependency resolution, preview and diff, state tracking, and the plumbing to hundreds of provider APIs underneath SST.
AWS alone exposes hundreds of resource types, each with its own create, update, and delete semantics.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge (pulumi-terraform-bridge) is Apache-2.0 licensed.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge was built specifically to let projects like SST reuse Terraform's ecosystem of providers with the Pulumi engine.
Pulumi's engine does not require a Pulumi account, a network call to Pulumi Cloud, or any Pulumi-hosted service to run.
Pulumi's Automation API works for teams embedding Pulumi programs inside their own tools, embedding the engine in the same way SST does.
The same provider bridge lets any Pulumi user consume Terraform providers directly.
Cross-reference: the post links to /blog/any-terraform-provider/, /docs/iac/concepts/automation-api/, and /docs/iac/get-started/terraform/terraform-providers/ as existing pages.
Nitric is a cloud-agnostic application framework whose docs state that "all of the direct deployment providers use Pulumi under the hood for their deployments."
Official Nitric providers are built directly on Pulumi's AWS, GCP, and Azure providers.
Defang deploys Docker Compose applications to the cloud, and its Pulumi provider README describes taking "a Compose file, translates it to a Pulumi program, and runs `pulumi up`".
Nitric, Defang, and SST all expose a narrower, more opinionated interface to their users while relying on the Pulumi engine and its provider bridge underneath.
Most SST users never write Pulumi code and work entirely in SST's component model.
Because SST's constructs compile to Pulumi resources, resources without a dedicated SST construct can be defined directly in Pulumi and deployed as part of the same SST app.
The latest SST release, v4.17.1, went out in July 2026.
The `sst` package on npm is pulling roughly 796,000 downloads a week (796,291 for the week of September 5-11, 2026).
SST's own team page credits the same team behind opencode, an open source AI coding agent.
The opencode GitHub repository (anomalyco/opencode) has a larger star count than SST's repository.
opencode has grown quickly since launch.
SST's dependency on the Pulumi engine has not changed and its release cadence has not changed as a result of the team's broadened attention to opencode.

Pulumi Cloud provides cross-team visibility into infrastructure state; policy as code provides guardrails a platform team can enforce centrally; components allow sharing infrastructure patterns across an organization.
Adopting Pulumi Cloud, policy as code, and components does not require leaving the Pulumi engine SST already uses.
SST does not invoke the Terraform CLI or write Terraform state; its Terraform providers are bridged through the Pulumi engine.
SST does not expose cross-team visibility, policy enforcement, or infrastructure sharing across more than one application on its own.
Cross-reference: the blog post /blog/aws-cdk-vs-pulumi-why-sst-switched/ tells the fuller story of SST's move off CDK from SST's side.
Cross-reference: /docs/iac/guides/basics/how-pulumi-works/ describes the engine mechanics.
